parties:
Malik Mehdi Kabir and anothers ----- Appellants
vs
Rabitat-al-Alam-al-Islami and others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J : These appeals, by leave, arise out of the same judgment and accordingly these appeals are disposed of analogously by this judgment. Points involved in these appeals are whether, an acquisition proceedings would abate under section 12 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinances, 1982 (the Ordinance) if the requiring body failed to deposit the compensation money within the stipulated period of one year from the date of decision of the acquiring authority, or from the date of award of compensation and secondly, a previous decision based on different cause of action and also on a provision of law which is not applicable will be barred by their principle of res judicata in a subsequent writ petition on the same subject matter. It would be profitable if we narrate the facts out of which these appeals arise. 

 2. Respondent No.1, Rabitat Al-Alam-al-Islami, (Rabitat) filed Writ Petition No. 2746 of 2001 challenging the Gazette Notification dated 17th May, 2001, by which, the writ respondent No 3 cancelled the proceedings of LA Case No. 1/89-90. The case of Rabitat, in short, is that it is a Non- Government International Islamic Organization providing assistance in the fields of education, culture, social welfare, health care etc. In 1989 it applied to the Government to arrange them 1(one) acre of land in exchange of money at Gazipur, for the purpose of establishment of it's building complex and the writ respondent No.2, the Deputy Commissioner, after fulfillment of the requirements approved the proposal and started LA Case No. 1/89-90. After receiving the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance, 6(six) objections were raised by the owners of the property within the stipulated time as per section 4(1) and the said 6(six) objections were heard by the Land Acquisition Officer on 9th July, 1990. The writ respondent No.2 approved the proposed acquisition on 17th July, 1990. Writ Respondent No.2 request- ed the Secretary, Ministry of Land to approve the proposed acquisition on 20th July 1990. The writ respondent No.2 finally approved the said acquisition on 18th August, 1990. On 28th August, 1990 the Land Acquisition Officer published a notice under section 6(1) of the Ordinance asking the affected persons to produce their claims of compensation and on 7th April, 199 L the writ respondent No. 2 estimated the price of disputed land at Taka 17,03,625.45, and on 21st April, 1991 the acquiring authority asked Rabitat to deposit the said compensation money with in 18th August, 1991, as per section 12(1) of the Ordinance. Rabitat by a letter dated 24th July, 1991 requested the writ respondent No.2 to extend the time up to 31st December, 1991 for depositing the said compensation money. Against the said letter the writ respondent No. 3 intimated that there was no scope to extend the time under the said Ordinance. Thereafter Rabitat deposited Taka 1,00,000 (Taka one lakh) on 18th August, 1991. The Land Acquisition Officer by a letter dated 7th October, 1991 requested Rabitat to pay the balance compensation money. 

 3. Thereafter on 23rd December, 1991 the award of compensation was prepared and the writ respondent No.3 issued notice under section 7(3) of the Ordinance, which was served upon the affected persons to receive their award of compensation. After delivery of possession writ respondent No.5 Dr Malik Mehdi Kabir and 2 others filed Writ Petition Nos. 462, 529 and 2639 of 1992 respectively, challenging the acquisition proceedings. All the said three Petitions were heard analogously and the Rules were discharged, by judgment and order dated 8th March, 1998. Against the said judgment and order the writ respondent No.7 preferred Civil Petition No. 829 of 1998 and the same was dismissed by this Division by judgment and order dated 19th August, 1999. The writ respondent No.3 thereupon cancelled the LA Case No. 1 of 1989-90, which was published in the Gazette Notification on 17th May, 2001. After publication of the said Gazette Notification, the writ respondent No.3 directed Rabitat on 12th June, 2001, to return the land to the owners. 

 4. Writ respondent Nos. 1, 5, 8, 9, 16, and 17 contested the writ petition by filing separate affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the petition and claimed that the impugned Notification was passed legally as Rabitat failed to deposit the compensation money within the stipulated time in accordance with law and therefore the proceedings stood abated. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties and by the impugned judgment made the rule absolute but it did not declare the impugned Gazette Notification, Annexure-S to the writ petition, canceling the acquisition of the disputed property in LA Case No. 1 of 1989-90 without lawful authority and also did not give direction upon the Deputy Commissioner to declare the acquisition of the property in the official Gazette under section 11 of the Ordinance as prayed. Therefore, the cancellation of the acquisition proceedings by the impugned Gazette Notification stands despite making the rule absolute. 

 6. When the earlier writ petitions were filed, the acquiring authority did not record order for abatement of the proceedings. On the point of abatement of the proceedings the High Court Division in the earlier Judgment observed the Deputy Commissioner as per provision of section 5 of the Ordinance made decision as regards acquisition on 18th August, 1990 vide Annexure B to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No.5. Award under section 7 for payment of compensation to the petitioners was made by the Deputy Commissioner on 8th April, 1991 and thereafter the requiring body deposited the entire amount of award on 23rd December, 1991. So it is seen that com pensation that to be 'paid' to the petitioners or to be 'deposited' in case of petitioners not accepting the same, in the public account as per provision of section 10 of the Ordinance was available with requiring body well within the period of one year as referred in section 12 of the Ordinance. This being the position of the view that contention of the petitioners that the requiring body did not deposit the amount awarded as compensation for payment to the petitioners within the period as referred to in section 12 of the Ordinance and consequent thereupon LA Case No.1 of 1989-90 started for acquiring petitioners' land stood abated is not well founded." 

 7. So, the decision of the High Court Division is based on the fact that the award for compensation was made on 8th April, 1991 and as the compensation money having been deposited by Rabitat on 12th December, 1991 within one year from the date of award for compensation, the deposit was made in time, the proceedings not abated. This finding is based on misconception of law, inasmuch as, the High Court Division made the above observation on the basis of the substituted section 12 of the Ordinance, which provision would not be applicable in the said writ petitions. The Deputy Commissioner after hearing objection approved the proposal of the Land Acquisition Officer under section 5 of the Ordinance by order dated 17th July, 1990. The earlier writ petitions were filed in 1992. In the premises, it is the unamended provisions of section 12- would hold the field but the High Court Division wrongly considered the amended provision. Section 12 as stood on the date of acquisition reads as follows: 

 "12. Abatement or Revocation of Acquisition Proceedings--(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, where in any case compensation has not been paid or deposited within a period of one year from the date of decision of the Government. [the Divisional Commissioner or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case may be, for acquisition of the property under section 5 or the proviso to section 4(3)(b), as the case may be], for no fault of the person interested, all proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of that period, stand abated and a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner to that effect shall be published in the official Gazette." 

 "12. Abatement or revocation of acquisition proceeding-Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, where in any case the estimated amount of the award of compensation has not been deposited by the requiring person for acquisition of any property under section 5 within the period specified in section 7(4), all proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of that period, stand abated and a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner to that effect shall be published in the Official Gazette." 

 9. There are substantial differences between these two provisions. The difference is that under the old provision the compensation has to be deposited within one year from the date of decision of the acquiring authority under section 5, whereas, under the new provision the compensation has to be deposited within one year from the date of making estimated amount of the award of compensation under section 7(4). Naturally the period of limitation to deposit the compensation would reckon from the date of the final decision regarding acquisition under the earlier provision, whereas, under the amended provision, the period would be counted from the date of award of compensation. Therefore, there is apparent error in the earlier judgment on the point of limitation to deposit the compensation which has resulted in the decision that the deposit has been made within a period of one year. The High Court Division was totally confused as to the applicability of the law during the relevant time and this might be due to the fact that when the writ petitions were disposed of on 8th March, 1998 the substituted provision of section 12 was in force. If this change of law was brought to the notice of the High Court Division, the decision would have been otherwise. While affirming the judgment this Division through looked at the change of law but dismissed the leave petition relying upon the views taken in Ministry of Land Administration vs Subash Chandra Das, 46 DLR (AD) 63 on the reasoning that "it is not the case of the petitioner (writ respondent No.7) that he was not paid compensation or that his compensation money was not deposited within one year from the date of decision to acquire under section 5 or proviso the section 4(3)(b) of the Ordinance". 

 11. Admittedly Rabitat did not deposit the compensation money in accordance with section 12(1) of the Ordinance is apparent from its statement in paragraph 3 of the concise statement wherein it is stated that "on 18th August, 1990, the Deputy Commissioner approved the acquisition" and "on 18th August, 1991, the respondent herein initially deposited Taka 1,00,000 (taka one lakh) by bank draft. Thereafter on 8th October, 1991 the LA Officer asked the respondent immediately to pay the rest of the money, i.e. Taka 16,03,647.45 (Taka sixteen lakh three thousand six hundred seventy four and fifty paisa) in favour of Deputy Commissioner, which the respondent paid by bank draft on 21st December, 1991," So, Rabitat admitted that the final decision regarding acquisition was made on 18th August, 1990 and as per section 12 Rabitat was required to deposit compensation within one year from the date of final decision regarding acquisition. This is the requirement of law and the Court has no power to hold otherwise. 

 "The provision of section 12 will come into play only when the compensation is not paid to the persons interested or not kept in a deposit account of the Public Account of the Republic under sub-section (1) of section 10. Under section 12 no obligation as such is placed on the requiring body to deposit compensation money within six months from the date of decision of acquisition." 

 "Under section 15, when any property is proposed to be acquired for any person other than the Government, such person shall enter into an agreement with the government in a prescribed form before a notice under section 3 is published. The Deputy Commissioner has to tender and pay compensation to "the persons interested", before taking possession, to be assessed in terms of sections 8 and 9. The payment of compensation is regulated by section 10. It is either "paid" in terms of section 10(1) or "deposited" in terms of section 10(2). It is this "payment" and "deposited" in section 10 which is attracted in section 12, not the deposit of compensation by the requiring body. Reading all the sections together, sections 8, 9, 10, 12 and 15, it is clear that abatement will take place if the acquiring authority fails to "pay" or "deposit" compensation in terms of section 10 within one year from the date of decision of the Government (which in section 5 in the case of acquisition) 

 14. In Subash Chandra Das two views have been expressed as regards the date of deposit of compensation by the requiring body. MH Rahman, J was of the opinion that no obligation is placed on the requiring body to deposit compensation within one year from the date of decision for acquisition where as, Mustafa Kamal, J, on the other hand, was of the opinion that the requiring body will deposit the compensation well ahead of expiry of one year from the date of final decision for acquisition. Let us now examine the correct position of law. Section 15(1) of the Ordinance provides that "when any property is proposed to be acquired for any person other than the Government, such person shall enter into an agreement with the Government in such form as may be prescribed before a notice under section 3 of the Ordinance is published." 

 15. The purpose for entering into such agreement is to initiate the process of acquisition so that the person on whose favour the land will be acquired gets possession from the Government on payment of compensation. The obligation of the requiring body under the agreement is to deposit compensation money within the time specified therein and the obligation of the acquiring authority is to acquire the land after performance of formalities and then to handover possession to the requiring body. If the latter does not deposit the compensation money within the specified time, the acquiring authority will not be able to pay the compensation to the affected person under section 10 and if the compensation is not paid, the Deputy Commissioner has no power to take possession from the affected person. The payment of compensation is a precondition for taking over possession of the land. Thus there is no scope on the part of the acquiring authority to complete the process of acquisition as per provisions of the Ordinance unless the requiring body deposits the compensation money as per agreement. It is only on payment of the compensation to the affected person the land or property "shall stand acquired and vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances" under section 11 of the Ordinance. The High Court Division did not express any independent opinion on the point of violation of sections 12 and 15 on simple reasons that this Division has settled the point in Subash Chandra Das and in Civil Petition No. 829 of 1998. 

 16. Section 5 of the Ordinance relates to the final decision regarding acquisition of land by the acquiring authority i.e. the Government or the Divisional Commissioner. The proviso to section 4(3)(b) authorizes the Deputy Commissioner to make decision about the acquisition of the property instead of submitting the records of the proceedings to the Divisional Commission if no objection is raised by any interested person in the property. It is admitted by the writ petitioner in its concise statement that six objections have been filed from persons interested in the property. Therefore, the Deputy Commissioner had no authority to give final decision regarding the acquisition under the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 4. In view of this admitted position of the case, the final decision regarding acquisition made by the Deputy Commissioner was also without jurisdiction. 

 17. Section 15 is a mandatory provision of law to be complied with by the requiring body before the acquiring authority proceeds for acquisition of the land if such acquisition is made not for public purposes of the Government but the question is when the compensation in to be deposited by the requiring body? As noticed above, there are conflicting opinions in Subash Chandra Das on this point. "The requiring body, therefore, will deposit the consideration money with the Government well ahead of expiry of one year from the date of decision of the Government, but within what date, is subject matter of agreement between the Government and the requiring body under section 15" argued by Mustafa Kamal, J. We would like to add that while fixing the date in the agreement it should be kept in mind sections 5, 10, 11 and 12, because if the requiring body does not deposit the compensation within a period of one year from the date of decision for acquisition, the proceedings shall stand abated. Secondly, how the Deputy Commissioner will take possession from the affected person unless the requiring body pays compensation? The possession will be delivered if it pays the compensation in time. 

 18. In view of the above, with due respect, we find ourselves unable to agree with the understanding of section 12 in Sub ash Chandra Das on the points as to whether there is obligation on the part of the requiring body to deposit the compensation, and whether on the .failure on the part of the requiring body to deposit the compensation within one year from the date of decision for acquisition, the proceedings of the acquisition shall stand abated. MH Rahman, J. argues that no obligation is placed on the requiring body to deposit the compensation money within one year (inadvertently mentioned within six months) from the date of decision of acquisition, while Mustafa Kamal, J. is of the opinion that the abatement will take place if the acquiring authority fails to payor deposit compensation in terms of section 10 within one year from the date of the decision of the Government. We find inconsistency in the above arguments. There is no ambiguity on a plain reading of section 12 that the obligation to pay or deposit the compensation within the specified date is upon the requiring body because if it defaults in complying with such obligation, the acquisition proceedings for the acquisition of the property which was started in its favour, shall stand abated. The Government is under no obligation to pay the compensation money to the affected person. 

 19. Section 12 is a non-obstante clause which contains the expression 'Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance. The provision containing such clause prevails despite anything to the contrary in the Ordinance is contained. When the non-obstante clause refers to the provision of a statute the intention of the legislature must be determined and the clause has to be construed accordingly. It is often used by way of abundant caution, but mainly used as a legislative device, in case of conflict, to give the provision containing non-obstante clause an overriding effect over any other provision. Therefore, there is no doubt that this provision will prevail other over provisions of the Ordinance. This section should not be read 'subject to' other provisions in the Ordinance. The arguments that no obligation is placed on the requiring body to deposit the compensation money within one year from the date of acquisition and that abatement will take place if the acquiring authority fails to pay or deposit the compensation in terms of section 10 are contrary to the mandate of law for, it is the obligation of the person for whose interest the land is acquired to deposit the compensation within time in order to avoid abatement. 

 22. The object of the Ordinance is to empower the acquiring authority to acquire land only for a public purpose affecting proprietary right of citizens. Article 42 (1) of the Constitution states subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property, and no property shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalized or requisitioned save by authority of law." The underlying idea of this provision is that a citizen shall not be deprived of his land otherwise than in accordance with law and if he is deprived of for public purpose, compensation at the market rate is given to him. No beneficial object of the acquisition can exonerate the government from the restrictions imposed by law and payment of compensation at the market rate. The Ordinance is required to be expounded liberally in favour of the citizen whose land acquired and strictly against the Government. When statutory rights of an exceptional character have been created the conditions prescribed by the statute for exercise of such rights should be strictly fulfilled. 

 24. On consideration of the relevant provisions our conclusion is that where the compensation has not been paid or deposited by the requiring body within a period of one year from the date of final decision of the acquiring authority for acquisition of the property under section 5 or the proviso to section 4 (3) (b), the proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of one year shall stand abated. Similar views have been taken by this Division in the review petition filed by Subash Chandra Das (50 DLR (AD) 106) against the earlier judgment reported in 46 DLR (AD) 63. This Division while disposing of the review petition accepted the contention of the learned counsel for the review petitioner observing that "as far as the exposition of section 12 is concerned, we entirely agree with Mr Pal that an acquisition proceeding shall stand abated if compensation has not been paid or deposited within 6 months (now one year) from the date of the decision of the authority concerned for acquisition of the property notwithstanding anything contained in the Ordinance", Therefore, there is no dispute that the requiring body was bound to deposit the compensation money within one year from date of the decision for acquisition. In this case the Deputy Commissioner approved the acquisition on 18th August, 1990, and as per provisions of law, Rabitat was required to deposit the compensation money within one year from that date but it failed to deposit the money within the statutory period and thus the proceedings stood abated on 17th August, 1991 by operation of law. 

 25. Section 12 states that in case of default on the part of the requiring body to deposit the compensation within the period mentioned therein the proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall 'stand abated'. A self executory expression has been used in the section for non-compliance of the obligation to deposit the compensation. The Deputy Commissioner in such case has no power to extend the time other than to publish in the Official Gazette the result of abatement of the proceedings. In other words, the acquisition proceedings will be put to an end and the Deputy Commissioner has no power to pass any order extending the time other than publishing the abatement order in the Official Gazette as soon as the period of one year expired. The Deputy Commissioner becomes functus Officio with regard to the said proceedings after the expiry of one year. He retains no power in the said proceedings. The intention of the legislature is clear that the abatement order will operate automatically without any further order of the Deputy Commissioner concerned. 

 27. Therefore, as soon as one year period expired from the date of final decision regarding acquisition if the requiring body fails to deposit compensation money the acquisition proceedings will automatically terminate. There is natural death of the acquisition proceedings and after its natural death there is no scope to revive this proceedings. In view of the above, we find no merit in the contention of Mr Abdur Razzaq that this Division having approved the views of the High Court Division, the proceedings have not been abated and that there is no scope to reopen the issue of abatement. The High Court Division, in the premises, committed the same error in holding that this point could not be reopened since it had been decided in the earlier cases. 

 28. As regards the point of res judicata, Mr Mahrnudul Islam contends that the findings of the High Court Division that the appellants in Civil Appeal No. 60 of 2006, who were not parties in the earlier writ petitions were also bound by the earlier decision, is based on misconception of law. Mr Islam argued that the earlier writ petitions were dismissed on the reasonings that it was not the case of the writ petitioners that they were not paid compensation or that the compensation money was not deposited within the statutory period but in this case, the point in issue is that the compensation money had not been deposited or paid within one year from the date of final decision regarding acquisition and thus, this point had not been heard and finally decided. We find substance in the contention of Mr Islam for, the question raised by these appellants was not considered by this Division in Civil Petition No. 829 of 1998 and the High Court Division in the earlier writ petitions. 

 30. In that case the writ petition was filed by a student of a medical college against order of principal striking off his name from college roll because he had not passed physics paper of B.Sc. Part-1 Examination. The petition impleading only principal and the state government was allowed on the ground of violation of the principles of natural justice. In the subsequent writ petition by the same student against order of the Registrar of University not allowing that student to appear in the 1st MBBS examination, the question arose whether the university was bound by the decision in previous writ petition. It was held that the principle of res judicata shall not apply. ID Dua, J. speaking for the Court argued : 

 31. We fail to understand how the High Court Division applied this case in the present case, which instead supporting the case of the writ petitioner supports the appellants? Though the point of abatement was decided in the earlier writ petition but the decision was given on a wrong premise of law. In AK Mahbub Co. vs State of MP AIR 1966 SC 1637.the question was whether the decision given the earlier case on the right of the parties visa vis an enactment would be res judicata in view of the change in law on the same subject. In the earlier decision it was held that contracts and agreements, such as the one held by the petitioner from were in essence and effect licences granted to the transferees to cut, gather and carry away, the produce in the shape of the tendu leaves, lac, or timber or wood". The decision was given in the light of Act 1 of 1951. Subsequently another legislation on the same subject was promulgated in 1964 namely, Madhya Pradesh Tendu Parra (Vypar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964 to make provisions for regulating in the public interest the trade of tendu leaves by creating State monopoly in such trade. The Division Commissioner then informed the petitioner firm that the right to collect tendu leaves was abrogated by the State Government. The writ petition was filed challenging the restriction. It was argued by Hidayatullah,J. as under: 

 32. The last point urged by Mr TH Khan is whether the acquisition of property for construction of office complex by a Non-government Organization is at all fall within the meaning of 'Public purpose' or 'public interest' within the meaning of section 3 of the Ordinance. Admittedly, Rabitat is a Non-Government Organization. This acquisition cannot be taken for public purpose within the meaning of section 3, which authorizes the Deputy Commissioner to issue notice for acquisition if any property is needed for "any public purpose" or in public interest". The entire scheme of the law is acquisition of the private property for public purpose. The power to acquire property is a power to acquire it only for a public purpose. There is no power in the acquiring authority to acquire private property in order to give it to private persons because if this process is allowed every Non-Government Organization, there are about a million or more working in the country, on influencing the Government or the Deputy Commissioner would acquire any private property for their office buildings. This is not the purpose of the law. 'Public purpose' is contained of the power itself. In Willoughby's constitutional law it is stated: 

 "As between individuals, no necessity, however great, no exigency, however imminent, no improvement, however valuable, no refusal, however unneighbourly, no obstinacy, however unreasonable, no offers of compensation, however extra vagrant, can compel or require any man to part with an inch of his estate. 

 35. In Hamabai Frangee vs Secretary of State, 421A 44 the judicial committee explained meaning of the word 'public purposes' as under: 

 36. The explanation public purpose, is therefore, construed according to the times in which particular legislation is enacted is so construed. The acquisition of the immovable property has to be held to have been made for a public purpose and not otherwise. In this particular case, it is seen that the acquisition has been made not for any public purpose rather it is meant for private purpose for office complex of a Non-Government Organization and the acquisition is not needed for public purpose. The High Court Division has totally over looked this aspect of the matter. 

 37. Both the appeals were filed by two sets of writ respondents against the same judgment of the writ petition which challenged the impugned Gazette Notification revoking the acquisition proceedings. We found that the writ respondent No.3 committed no illegality in revoking the proceedings in respect of acquisition of the land. Therefore, the decision in one appeal will cover the other appeal as well.
